strengths: Well-grounded framework with clear connection to Polya's problem-solving theory and cognitive science foundations
Dual-granularity annotation (sentence and paragraph level) reveals complementary structural insights at different reasoning scales
Comprehensive experimental design comparing diverse tasks (mathematical vs. factual reasoning) and multiple models with varying capabilities
High inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa = 0.89) demonstrating annotation quality
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (transition heatmaps and state graphs) that communicate framework utility
Interesting task-specific insights about goal-oriented mathematical reasoning vs. evidence-driven scientific reasoning
Honest acknowledgment of framework limitations including discretization, annotation bias, and fixed taxonomy constraints
weaknesses: Limited empirical scale with only 30 AIME and 50 GPQA examples—too small to support generalizable claims; lacks error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing
Annotation methodology relies entirely on GPT-4o-mini with only 10% manual verification, insufficient to validate systematic biases or ensure reproducibility across model versions

Fundamental FSM framework limitations inadequately addressed: memoryless assumption acknowledged but not explored despite potential problems for sequential reasoning; formal definition of alphabet (Σ) is non-standard and circular; transition function formalism (δ: Q × Σ → P(Q)) is defined but ignored in practice
All seven proposed applications in Discussion section (controllability, error localization, training feedback, etc.) are entirely unvalidated with zero experimental demonstration

Limited novelty: straightforward application of FSM to reasoning traces yielding primarily intuitive insights (strong models explore more, weak models finish early) with no new algorithms or control mechanisms

Methodological concerns: self-loop removal lacks justification and may lose information about reasoning redundancy; inadequate discussion of sentence vs. paragraph granularity trade-offs; highly task-specific findings with unclear generalization to other domains
Correlation vs. causation not addressed: paper shows longer FSM chains correlate with AIME accuracy but doesn't establish whether length causes performance or merely reflects model capacity
Missing ablations and comparisons: no alternative annotation schemes compared, no taxonomy ablations, no user studies validating FSM representation quality against human understanding
Lacks failure analysis: no investigation of when FSM framework breaks down or produces misleading insights for non-conforming reasoning patterns

strengths: Well-motivated research problem addressing understanding of LLM reasoning processes
Clear formal FSM framework with explicit mapping to reasoning dynamics
Principled annotation methodology with transparency (prompts provided, inter-annotator agreement reported)
Dual-granularity analysis (sentence and paragraph levels) enabling multi-scale insights
Effective visualizations (state distributions, transition heatmaps, state graphs)
Some interesting task-dependent findings (mathematical vs. factual reasoning have different characteristics)
weaknesses: Critical annotation methodology flaw: entire dataset annotated by LLM (GPT-4o-mini) with only 10% human validation; no sensitivity analysis for annotation errors
Significant gap between claims and content: title promises 'hierarchical thinking' but FSMs represent only linear sequences without hierarchical structure
Limited technical novelty: framework largely reformulates Polya's 1945 problem-solving steps with minor additions; straightforward state categorization rather than mechanistic modeling
Fundamental model limitation acknowledged but unaddressed: memoryless FSMs cannot capture context-dependent reasoning progression; paper concedes pushdown automata would be better
Insufficient empirical scope: only 30 AIME + 50 GPQA problems (80 total), 3 models; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance quantification
Speculative applications without evidence: Section 5 claims FSM analysis enables controllability, error localization, robustness but provides zero experimental validation

Analysis largely confirms intuitions rather than providing novel insights: longer reasoning helps math problems (expected), better models manage uncertainty (predictable), distributed transitions (intuitive)
Lacks comparison with alternative CoT analysis methods; no ablation studies justifying choice of 6 states; no empirical validation of framework optimality
Small validation set (10%) for annotation quality; no human-only baseline; missing details on disagreement resolution
Correlation vs. causation unclear: longer FSM sequences correlate with AIME accuracy but causation not established; dataset-level aggregation of transitions loses problem-specific structure
No code availability mentioned; reproducibility concerns (unusual temperature 1e-19 unjustified, dated model versions)
Ambiguous state definitions: 'augment-refine' vs. uncertainty-driven backtracking overlap; inter-rater reliability only reported at aggregate level (κ=0.89), not for subcategories
Results generalization unclear: only math/science tasks; applicability to other reasoning domains unknown
Missing critical experiments: per-problem analysis relating FSM to correctness, sensitivity to annotation approaches, demonstration of claimed applications, larger-scale evaluation, ablation studies

strengths: Well-motivated FSM framework grounded in cognitive science theory (Polya) with clear formalization and mapping to LLM reasoning
Comprehensive empirical analysis across multiple models and granularities with thorough state frequency, transition probability, and FSM length metrics
Nuanced finding that reasoning optimality is task-dependent: mathematical reasoning requires longer trajectories for precision, while scientific reasoning shows saturation effects
Good reproducibility practices including detailed annotation prompts, inter-annotator agreement (0.89 Cohen's Kappa), fixed random seeds, and hyperparameter specifications
Clear presentation with well-defined six-state taxonomy and effective visualizations of state distributions and transition patterns
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: only 80 total problems across two datasets, two task types, and three models; results may not generalize to other domains or closed-source models; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Annotation quality concerns: relies entirely on LLM auto-labeling with minimal manual verification; no analysis of annotation error patterns or their impact on conclusions; complex prompts may introduce systematic bias

Lack of practical validation: all applications in Discussion are speculative with no concrete experiments; no comparison with prior categorization work (Li et al., Bogdan et al., Lee et al.) or ablation studies showing FSM benefits

Limited theoretical depth: descriptive rather than explanatory; causality unclear between adaptive patterns and performance; memoryless FSM acknowledged but not adequately justified; discretization into 6 states loses information

Methodological limitations: self-loop removal not well justified; unclear whether six-state taxonomy is universal or inductively derived from these specific models; no analysis of how state transitions depend on reasoning history despite sequential nature

strengths: Novel FSM abstraction provides elegant bridge between interpretability and control over reasoning trajectories, addressing genuine gap in prior work

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 models, 4 benchmarks with rigorous validation: Markov assumption verified (82.1% sign agreement), annotation quality confirmed (Kappa=0.89), robustness analysis on false boundaries
Practically significant efficiency gains: 25× fewer interventions while maintaining/improving accuracy demonstrates identification of high-leverage intervention points
Thorough and honest limitations discussion including correlation-causation gap, domain specificity, cross-model generalization, and model-specific dependency
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, annotation prompts, examples of annotated CoTs provided, code availability promised
weaknesses: Fundamental correlation-causation problem remains unresolved: Transition Advantage Matrix identifies statistical associations but steering cannot compensate for model's missing domain knowledge; rescue rates vary 8.9-47.9% without clear predictive factors

State taxonomy lacks principled justification: Six states chosen post-hoc for math/science tasks with no systematic ablation on granularity; generalization to other domains speculative; Uncertainty Estimation/Backtracking distinction difficult in practice

Severe limitations on generalization: cross-model steering is 1% worse with 10× higher interventions (Table 2); distilled models show negligible gains (Table 7); domain-specific to math/science QA with binary success signals

Sentence-level granularity creates significant blind spots: 84-99.6% false boundary rates from ellipsis tokens; confidence gating mitigates but doesn't eliminate (0.1-18.9% slip-through); no principled solution offered

Q-Value iteration on noisy empirical data: requires ad-hoc reward clipping without justification; second-order analysis shows minimal benefits suggesting crude R matrix or true Markov property violation unresolved

Automated annotation bias: GPT-4o-mini used for labeling (11% disagreement rate); error propagates through pipeline; only 10% human validation; qualitative examples in Figure 3 potentially cherry-picked
Gains diminish significantly on easier tasks: +13% AIME25 vs +0.2-0.7% GSM8K; on tasks with 94%+ baseline accuracy, improvements negligible; method appears tuned to high-difficulty reasoning regimes
Missing critical comparisons: no direct comparison to Chen et al. (2025a) despite citing as motivation; no comparison to process reward models or fine-tuning baselines; unclear relative merit

strengths: Intuitive FSM framework connecting to classical cognitive theory (Polya, Schoenfeld), providing a cleaner abstraction than token-level analysis
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 benchmarks and 3-4 state-of-the-art models with detailed ablations and qualitative examples
Practical efficiency gains: 25× fewer interventions (MATH-500) with consistent improvements, showing method identifies high-leverage decision points
Thorough documentation: extensive appendices with implementation details, prompts, annotation guidelines, failure analysis supporting reproducibility
Honest acknowledgment of fundamental limitations (correlation ≠ causation, Markov assumption, annotation bias) upfront in main text
weaknesses: Critical soundness issue: Transition Advantage Matrix R captures correlation (successful transitions) not causation (transitions that cause success). Paper acknowledges but doesn't address with causal experiments (no counterfactuals, ablations forcing negative-R transitions, or mediation analysis)

Sentence boundary detection fundamentally flawed: false boundary rates of 84.73%-90.23% with slip-through rates of 6.7%-18.9% after confidence gating, undermining where steering interventions actually occur

Markov assumption problematic: first-order model cannot capture long-range reasoning dependencies; Appendix C's validation weak (82.1% sign agreement isn't proof; offline Q-values applied online violate stationarity assumption)

State abstraction is coarse (6 states insufficient for non-math domains), domain-specific, and lacks systematic evaluation of granularity trade-offs; single-label-per-sentence rule oversimplifies mixed-function statements
Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (difference-of-means steering, orthogonal injection, triplet loss, Q-learning on 6-state FSM is trivial); main contribution is FSM abstraction

Empirical gains modest and task-dependent: collapse on easier tasks (GSM8K: +0.23%), poor cross-model transfer (distilled DeepSeek-R1: +0.4%), no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals (single seed 42)

Missing critical comparisons: no evaluation against other control methods (Chen et al. 2025a, Venhoff et al. 2025), greedy steering sometimes degrades performance without explanation, prompt-based steering not fully explored
Code unavailable (blank URL despite claims); hyperparameter choices appear ad-hoc (δ=0.06, α∈[0.1,1.2], γ=0.9, 100 iterations); Appendix J shows high sensitivity to α

Rescue/harm rates in Table 8 conflate helpful interventions with counterfactual failures; no true causal evidence beyond association; Table 1 shows Q-Value sometimes increases tokens despite efficiency claims

Limited scope: requires binary success signal (can't evaluate open-ended tasks directly); advantage matrices dataset-specific with no cross-dataset transfer evaluation; method primarily helps natively-trained reasoners, not practical distilled models

strengths: Novel FSM abstraction of reasoning with sound mathematical formulation grounded in classical problem-solving theory (Pólya, Schoenfeld)
Principled planning-aware control method using Q-value iteration, providing theoretically motivated alternative to heuristic steering
Comprehensive experimental validation: 3 models × 4 benchmarks with thorough ablations on Markov assumption (82% sign agreement), hyperparameter sensitivity, and intervention effectiveness
Practical efficiency gain: 25× reduction in interventions compared to greedy baselines while maintaining or improving accuracy
Strong technical execution including orthogonal steering injection to preserve content-aligned components and confidence-aware gating that reduces harm rate to 0.4-15.8%
Excellent presentation with clear figures, informative examples, and extensive reproducibility-supporting appendices (annotation prompts, hyperparameters, annotated examples)
Honest and thorough limitations discussion acknowledging fundamental constraints (Markov assumption, correlation vs. causation, coarse abstraction, domain specificity)
weaknesses: Fundamental Markov assumption limitation: FSM cannot capture longer-range dependencies; second-order analysis shows minimal improvement (mostly neutral/negative), questioning whether richer models are actually beneficial

Causality vs. correlation gap: Transition Advantage Matrix identifies correlations not causal effects; steering cannot overcome knowledge gaps—bounded by model's baseline capabilities, acknowledged but not resolved

Limited generalization: weak cross-model transferability (Table 2 shows 0.4-0.6% accuracy drop; intervention cost increases substantially); taxonomy domain-specific to math/science; one model shows minimal gains (Table 7)

Coarse state abstraction (6 states) may oversimplify reasoning; no systematic ablation on alternative granularities; unmeasured impact of annotation edge cases (mixed-function sentences, epistemic hedging)

Sentence-boundary intervention constraint: high false boundary rates (84.73%-90.23%, mostly ellipsis); slipthrough rates remain 6.7%-18.9% despite confidence gating; cannot intervene at mid-sentence critical points
Modest improvements on high-baseline tasks: GSM8K improvements marginal (94.39%→94.62% GPT-L); QWEN on AIME25 shows greedy steering degradation (83.33%→76.67%), indicating policy suboptimality
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single random seed; limited characterization of result variance

Incomplete experimental analysis: no comparison with other reasoning interpretability methods; limited ablation of when different strategies help; DeepSeek-R1 underperformance (Table 7) under-analyzed

Reproducibility concerns: code URL not provided; state assignment relies on GPT-4o-mini with specific temperature prone to model-update obsolescence; layer selection requires empirical search lacking principled justification
State taxonomy development not fully justified: process of arriving at 6 states unclear; connection to Pólya/Schoenfeld is intuitive but post-hoc; no quantitative comparison of alternative taxonomies
